questions.q: What naming convention do PowerShell cmdlets follow?
options: Verb-Noun (e.g. Get-Process, Set-Item), making their purpose predictable and easy to guess
snake_case function names only
Random abbreviations with no consistent pattern
Noun-Verb ordering (e.g. Process-Get)
questions.explain: Every built-in cmdlet follows Verb-Noun, using a small standardized set of approved verbs (Get, Set, New, Remove, etc.), which makes it possible to guess a cmdlet's likely name and behavior once you know the pattern.

questions.q: What does Get-Help <cmdlet> -Examples show?
options: Only the cmdlet's syntax, with no examples
Sample usage of the cmdlet drawn from its help documentation, showing common invocation patterns
The cmdlet's full .NET source code
A list of unrelated cmdlets
questions.explain: The -Examples switch narrows Get-Help's output to just the EXAMPLES section of a cmdlet's help, which is often the fastest way to see a working invocation without reading the full syntax and parameter reference.

questions.q: What is a fundamental difference between PowerShell's pipeline and a traditional Unix-style shell's pipeline (like bash)?
options: PowerShell pipes pass structured .NET objects between cmdlets, preserving properties and methods, rather than plain text that must be re-parsed
PowerShell only supports plain text piping, just like bash
bash pipes pass full objects while PowerShell only passes text
They are functionally identical in this respect
questions.explain: Because PowerShell is built on .NET, the pipeline moves live objects with their properties and methods intact, so downstream commands can reference a specific property (like $_.Name) directly instead of parsing text output.

questions.q: What does the pipeline operator | do in PowerShell?
options: Comments out the rest of the line
Declares a new variable
Sends the output objects of one cmdlet as input to the next cmdlet
Escapes special characters in a string
questions.explain: The pipe operator chains commands together by taking the output object(s) of the command on its left and feeding them in as input to the command on its right.

questions.q: How do you declare a variable in PowerShell, and what's notable about its typing?
options: Variables must be declared with var name; and are always strings
PowerShell has no variables, only pipeline objects
Variables require an explicit type declaration on every single use, with no default typing
$name = value; PowerShell variables are loosely/dynamically typed by default but can be explicitly cast, e.g. [int]$x = 5
questions.explain: PowerShell variables are prefixed with $ and are dynamically typed based on the assigned value by default, but you can constrain a variable to a specific .NET type with an explicit cast like [int] or [string].

questions.q: When would you use VS Code with the PowerShell extension over the built-in Windows PowerShell ISE?
options: Cross-platform editing with modern extensions, IntelliSense, and an integrated terminal, especially important since the ISE doesn't support PowerShell 7+ (Core)
ISE is only for viewing scripts and VS Code cannot run scripts at all
There is no difference; they are the same product under different names
VS Code cannot debug PowerShell scripts at all
questions.explain: The ISE is a legacy, Windows-only editor tied to Windows PowerShell 5.1 and is no longer actively developed; VS Code with the PowerShell extension supports PowerShell 7+, runs cross-platform, and gets ongoing feature updates.

questions.q: What's the difference between Where-Object and Select-Object?
options: They do the exact same thing in PowerShell
Where-Object filters which objects pass through the pipeline based on a condition; Select-Object chooses which properties (or how many objects) to keep from those that pass through
Select-Object filters rows while Where-Object picks columns
Where-Object can only be used with numeric values
questions.explain: Where-Object is a filter — it decides which objects continue down the pipeline based on a test condition. Select-Object reshapes what continues, by picking specific properties or limiting how many objects pass through (e.g. -First 5).

questions.q: What does Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 do?
options: Lists all processes alphabetically by name
Kills the top 5 CPU-consuming processes
Lists the 5 processes using the least CPU
Lists the 5 processes using the most CPU, sorted highest to lowest
questions.explain: Sort-Object CPU -Descending orders the process objects from highest CPU usage to lowest, and Select-Object -First 5 then keeps only the first five objects from that sorted list — the five heaviest CPU consumers.

questions.q: Why does Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} work cleanly, in a way a plain text tool couldn't easily replicate without extra parsing?
options: Because Where-Object secretly converts every object to text first
Because $_ always refers to a fixed global variable rather than the current piped item
Because Get-Service emits actual ServiceController objects with a real Status property, so $_.Status is a structured property lookup rather than string pattern matching
Because PowerShell requires manually converting Status to a string before comparing it
questions.explain: Since PowerShell objects carry real, typed properties, filtering on $_.Status is a direct property comparison rather than needing to pattern-match against formatted text output, which is fragile if the display format ever changes.

questions.q: What does ForEach-Object do differently from a foreach statement?
options: They are exactly identical with no behavioral difference
foreach can only be used with numbers
ForEach-Object cannot access the current pipeline object via $_
ForEach-Object is a pipeline cmdlet that processes objects one at a time as they arrive from the pipeline (streaming); a foreach statement operates on an already-materialized collection in memory
questions.explain: ForEach-Object receives items from the pipeline and processes each one as it arrives, which is more memory-efficient for large streams; the foreach language keyword instead requires the full collection to already exist in memory before looping starts.

questions.q: What's typically required to actually execute a .ps1 script file in a fresh PowerShell session on a locked-down Windows machine?
options: The script's shebang line at the top of the file
An execution policy that permits running scripts (e.g. RemoteSigned or Bypass), since PowerShell's default policy on Windows can block unsigned scripts
Compiling the script into an .exe first
Nothing; .ps1 scripts always run regardless of policy
questions.explain: Windows PowerShell ships with an execution policy (often Restricted by default) intended to reduce the risk of running untrusted scripts. Running a .ps1 file typically requires that policy be relaxed, at least for the current session or user.

questions.q: What does a switch statement in PowerShell allow that a long chain of if/elseif often doesn't as cleanly?
options: Nothing; they are functionally identical in every case
Matching a single value against multiple discrete cases — including wildcard and regex matching — in a more readable structure than a long if/elseif chain
Running the code in a completely separate PowerShell session
Skipping all variable declarations in the script
questions.explain: switch is built for testing one value against many possible cases, and PowerShell's switch additionally supports wildcard and regular-expression matching per case, which a plain if/elseif chain has to reimplement manually.

questions.q: What's the difference between foreach and while loops in PowerShell?
options: while can only ever run its block once
foreach requires no collection to iterate over
foreach iterates over each item in a known collection; while repeats a block as long as a condition remains true, which may not have a fixed number of iterations
foreach and while cannot both exist in the same script
questions.explain: foreach is built for stepping through a defined collection item by item. while is condition-driven and keeps looping as long as its test evaluates true, which suits situations where the number of iterations isn't known ahead of time.

questions.q: In a PowerShell function, what does the param() block define?
options: The function's return value only
The function's help documentation exclusively
The number of times the function is allowed to be called
The function's declared input parameters, including their types and any default values
questions.explain: param() is where a function declares the parameters callers can pass in, optionally with type constraints, default values, and attributes like [Parameter(Mandatory=$true)].

questions.q: What must you typically do before running Az module cmdlets against your Azure subscription in a new PowerShell session?
options: Nothing; Az module cmdlets work against your subscription with no authentication step
Authenticate with Connect-AzAccount (interactively or with a service principal), which establishes the session's Azure context
Install a separate license key for every individual cmdlet
Az cmdlets only work from inside the Azure Portal, never from a local session
questions.explain: Connect-AzAccount signs the session in to Azure and sets up the Az context (subscription, tenant, credentials) that every subsequent Az cmdlet in that session relies on.

questions.q: What is dbatools, in the context of running SQL Server tasks from PowerShell?
options: A T-SQL-only tool with no PowerShell involvement
A replacement for SQL Server Management Studio's GUI, and nothing else

A community PowerShell module providing hundreds of cmdlets for SQL Server administration (backups, migrations, configuration) that wrap T-SQL and SMO so you don't hand-write raw ADO.NET calls for every task
A Microsoft-official module bundled by default with every Windows installation
questions.explain: dbatools is a widely used open-source PowerShell module that packages common SQL Server DBA operations — backup/restore, migrations, configuration checks — as cmdlets, saving DBAs from writing low-level connection and query code themselves.

questions.q: What does Get-AzResourceGroup return when run after connecting to Azure?
options: A single string containing just the subscription's name
Nothing, unless the command is run from inside the Azure Portal
The Azure billing invoice for the current month
Objects representing the resource groups in the current subscription/context, which can then be piped into other cmdlets or inspected for properties
questions.explain: Like most Az cmdlets, Get-AzResourceGroup returns structured objects (with properties like ResourceGroupName and Location), not plain text, so the result can be filtered, sorted, or piped straight into another Az cmdlet.

questions.q: When automating a routine admin task with PowerShell (e.g. checking disk space across servers and emailing a report if low), what's a key benefit over doing it manually?
options: Manual admin work is always faster than any script
PowerShell scripts cannot be scheduled to run automatically
It can be run unattended and repeatably (e.g. via Task Scheduler), consistently applying the same logic every time rather than relying on a human to remember and execute the steps
Automation eliminates the need to ever test the script
questions.explain: The value of automation is consistency and reliability — a scheduled script runs the exact same checks on the exact same schedule without depending on a person remembering to do it, and it scales to many servers at once.

questions.q: When reading an unfamiliar PowerShell script you need to modify, what's a reliable first step to understand what it does?
options: Delete the script and start writing a replacement from scratch
Run it against production immediately to see what happens
Read through its param() block, look for the cmdlets it calls, and trace the pipeline/variable flow to understand inputs, outputs, and side effects before changing anything
Ignore the comments, since they are never accurate
questions.explain: Understanding a script's inputs (param block), what it actually does step by step, and what it changes or outputs is the safest way to modify it correctly without accidentally breaking existing behavior or causing unintended side effects.

questions.q: Why might a script use -WhatIf when calling a cmdlet like Remove-Item, or a custom function that supports it?
options: -WhatIf permanently deletes the target immediately, faster than normal
-WhatIf shows what the cmdlet would do without actually performing the action, which is useful for safely previewing destructive operations before running them for real
-WhatIf disables the cmdlet entirely and produces no output at all
-WhatIf only works with Get- cmdlets, never with state-changing ones
questions.explain: -WhatIf is a built-in safety mechanism for cmdlets that support ShouldProcess: it prints what the command would do without actually executing the change, which is especially valuable before running something destructive like a bulk delete.
